items.title: Native LSP client subsystem inventory
items.statement: Puppet Master owns a native LSP client architecture spanning host, supervision, sessions, registries, workspace and document resolution, synchronization, request brokerage, capabilities, diagnostics, language intelligence, and tracing.

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Puppet Master owns the LSP client architecture through host, supervisor, session, registry, workspace resolver, document store, sync engine, request broker, capability registry, diagnostics store, intelligence facade, and trace service, with conservative protocol lifecycle and FileSafe routing for mutation-capable edits.

items.title: Protocol lifecycle and mutation routing guardrails
items.statement: The required protocol ordering is initialize, initialized, normal traffic, shutdown, and exit; mutation-capable rename, format, code action, and workspace edits must route through FileSafe.

evidence.exact_quote: - initialize -> initialized -> normal traffic -> shutdown -> exit
- Rename, format, code action, and workspace edits always route through FileSafe.

items.title: Subsystem interfaces and data flow are unspecified
items.statement: LSPS-013 names the architecture components but does not define their individual responsibilities, call direction, input/output types, persistence boundaries, or error ownership, leaving multiple incompatible decompositions compliant with the requirement.
items.impact: Builders cannot derive stable interfaces or determine which component is authoritative for session, document, capability, diagnostic, and request state.
items.builder_discretion: Component APIs, dependency direction, data ownership, and consistency rules are wholly discretionary.

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: Puppet Master owns the LSP client architecture through host, supervisor, session, registry, workspace resolver, document store, sync engine, request broker, capability registry, diagnostics store, intelligence facade, and trace service, with conservative protocol lifecycle and FileSafe routing for mutation-capable edits.

items.title: Lifecycle transitions lack failure and cancellation semantics
items.statement: The lifecycle sequence is preserved as a token, but the window does not specify transition guards, initialization timeout behavior, cancellation, crash handling, shutdown failure handling, or when exit may be forced.
items.impact: Different clients can hang, leak processes, accept traffic too early, or terminate servers inconsistently.
items.builder_discretion: Timeouts, retry/kill policy, legal transition guards, and recovery states are left to implementation.

evidence.exact_quote: - initialize -> initialized -> normal traffic -> shutdown -> exit

items.title: Dynamic-registration enablement gate is not testable
items.statement: Dynamic registration is disabled until unregister handling exists, but no required unregister behaviors, state cleanup rules, race handling, or acceptance oracle defines when the gate may be lifted.
items.impact: The feature can remain permanently disabled or be enabled on an incomplete interpretation of unregister support.
items.builder_discretion: The meaning of 'handle /unregister' and the evidence sufficient to enable registration are unspecified.

evidence.exact_quote: - Dynamic registration stays disabled until PM can handle /unregister.

items.title: FileSafe routing has no apply-edit transaction contract
items.statement: Mandatory FileSafe routing is explicit, but the window does not define the edit request and result shapes, authority checks, preview/approval boundary, atomicity, conflict handling, rollback, partial failure, or error propagation.
items.impact: Mutation-capable LSP features could differ in safety, user authority, and data-loss behavior while still claiming FileSafe routing.
items.builder_discretion: All transaction, authorization, failure, and recovery semantics between LSP and FileSafe remain open.

evidence.exact_quote: - Rename, format, code action, and workspace edits always route through FileSafe.
- apply-edit paths

items.title: OpenCode compatibility inputs and rejected behaviors
items.statement: OpenCode registry patterns inform server definitions, stdio transport, lazy spawn, root discovery, and Assistant diagnostic context, while uncontrolled downloads, duplicate processes, weak status visibility, and unbounded backoff are rejected.

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: OpenCode-style registry findings are compatibility input for built-in/custom definitions, stdio transport, lazy spawn, root discovery, and diagnostics into Assistant context, while full-buffer or disk resync, uncontrolled auto-downloads, process duplication, weak status visibility, and unbounded backoff are rejected.

items.title: Rejected OpenCode behaviors lack enforceable operating policies
items.statement: The rejected behaviors are named but no download authorization flow, duplicate detection key, status visibility minimum, backoff bounds, eviction triggers, or recovery response makes the prohibition operationally testable.
items.impact: Implementations may reproduce the prohibited behavior under different labels or choose materially different limits and remediation.
items.builder_discretion: Authorization UX, identity/deduplication, visibility, retry limits, eviction, and operator recovery are unspecified.

evidence.exact_quote: - PM must not copy weak OpenCode behavior such as uncontrolled auto-downloads, duplicate sessions/processes, weak status visibility, or unbounded backoff.

items.title: Adjacent-tool ownership boundary is preserved
items.statement: LSP integration must preserve run-scoped tool events, mutation capability separation, formatter ownership, non-triggering host writes, plugin telemetry, workspace routing, and resolver inputs without bypassing adjacent tool subsystems.

evidence.exact_quote: canonical_text: LSP internal-tool boundaries preserve run-scoped tool event records, mutation_capable apply-edit separation, formatter-vs-LSP ownership, DAE non-triggering host writes, plugin/tool telemetry, workspace-tab routing, and resolver-priority inputs without bypassing adjacent tool subsystems.

items.title: Tool-event schemas and ownership precedence are absent
items.statement: The boundary names run_id, tool.invoked, mutation_capable, formatter-vs-LSP ownership, telemetry, workspace routing, apply-edit, and resolver-priority inputs, but does not define event schemas, ordering/idempotency, owner precedence, or conflict adjudication.
items.impact: Adjacent subsystems can double-handle, bypass, reorder, or disagree over the same operation and telemetry record.
items.builder_discretion: Event payloads, correlation, ownership precedence, and conflict behavior remain discretionary.

evidence.exact_quote: - run_id
- tool.invoked
- Formatter, plugin, telemetry, policy, workspace-tab, multi-project, mutation-capable, and apply-edit paths must not bypass one another.

items.title: ESLint v10 diagnostics support
items.statement: ESLint is the primary JavaScript-family lint and diagnostics LSP with v10 flat-config root discovery, Problems and Assistant integration, and JavaScript/TypeScript preset alignment.

items.title: ESLint discovery, launch, and recovery behavior is incomplete
items.statement: The unit identifies accepted flat-config filenames and Node ranges but does not specify root-search precedence, multi-config selection, server acquisition/launch inputs, missing or incompatible Node handling, restart behavior, or user-visible recovery.
items.impact: The same workspace can select different roots or fail differently across hosts, with no deterministic diagnostic or remediation contract.

items.title: Host-aware lazy-spawn process identity
items.statement: The OpenCode reference supplies registry and nearest-root patterns, while Puppet Master requires lazy initialization of one supervised process per host, server, and root identity with configuration, environment, and initialization options.

dimension_assessments.summary: The window states the principal native-client, compatibility, tool-boundary, ESLint, Slint, process, and Rust-stack behaviors, while detailed gaps are separately recorded.
Named capabilities cover core client services, JavaScript-family diagnostics, Slint language intelligence, process supervision, and async stdio client support.
Some inputs are named, but component, mutation, tool-event, server-launch, settings, and async-client input/output contracts remain unspecified.
Lifecycle ordering and major boundary rules are explicit, but component APIs, FileSafe transactions, cross-tool events, supervision, and client selection contracts are incomplete.
A protocol sequence and lazy-spawn model are named, but transition guards, registration readiness, failure states, preview states, and supervised-session recovery are missing.
FileSafe and adjacent subsystems are named as authority boundaries, but authorization, precedence, and conflict adjudication are not defined.
Document-level ownership is explicit, while runtime ownership among components and adjacent tool subsystems remains insufficiently allocated.
The editor, Problems panel, Assistant context, Settings, Slint files, JavaScript-family projects, and optional custom servers are identifiable consumers.
GUI-related units identify Problems, Assistant, Settings, and live preview, but lack interaction-complete visible-state and recovery contracts.
Protocol, FileSafe, server discovery, preview, supervision, compatibility, and backoff failures lack deterministic recovery semantics.
Mutation routing provides a safety boundary, but its authority contract is incomplete and diagnostics-to-Assistant transfer lacks privacy and minimization rules.
The reviewed units expose no dependency or unblock edges for their actual cross-unit prerequisites and downstream consumers.
Operational intent exists for lazy spawn, supervision, visibility, and bounded backoff, but executable policies for launch, status, retry, eviction, restart, and remediation are absent.
One-process identity and lazy spawn constrain gross duplication, but no capacity, latency, resource, queue, diagnostic, or trace budgets exist.
OpenCode input boundaries, Node compatibility, and ESLint v10 flat-config direction are explicit, but existing-project migration and mixed-version behavior are unspecified.
Listed validation proves planning-artifact integrity, not the runtime, failure, privacy, GUI, or performance requirements in the canonical text.
Consequential discretion remains across component APIs, state machines, transactions, cross-tool precedence, GUI states, process supervision, client libraries, privacy, and performance.
The unresolved async client stack is an explicit unknown, and several gates and terms lack criteria precise enough for one deterministic interpretation.
